Based on the retrieved healthcare Q&A matches, it appears that instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs) can be a useful addition to the diagnostic process in a memory clinic setting when considering dementia at 1- and 2-year follow-up. IADL disability is often identified as a risk factor for developing dementia.

In essence, IADL disability indicates an individual's ability to perform tasks that are typically necessary for daily living but may require assistance with certain activities, such as cooking, managing finances, or using the internet. When combined with other diagnostic tools and assessments, IADLs can provide valuable insights into a person's cognitive function and risk of developing dementia.

For example, in one study, higher levels of IADL disability were associated with an increased risk of cognitive decline at 1- and 2-year follow-up. Similarly, another study found that language deficits, particularly anomia (difficulty naming objects), may be relatively frequent in individuals with MND (Motor Neuron Disease) who have IADLs.

Therefore, incorporating IADL disability into the diagnostic process for dementia can help healthcare professionals identify individuals at higher risk and provide targeted interventions to support their care.
